Causative Get and Have: Get + -ed: Active and Passive
You use get and have in both active and passive structures.
The active pattern conveys the meaning of ‘cause or order someone to do something'. The form is:

get + person + to - infinitive OR
have + person + infinitive without to

For example:
I'll get the secretary to put in an order.
I'll have the secretary put in an order.

The passive pattern conveys the meaning of ‘arrange somebody else to do something'. The form is:

get/have + object + past participle

For example:
I will have/get my car fixed.
In this case, it means that somebody else will fix the car.
I'll have the janitor inspect the lightning in the office.
I'll get the employees to test out the lighting levels.
I'll have them move to different offices.
Denise will have the bulbs changed in the office.
Boris has given me the green light to proceed with this.
I had to get new bulbs shipped to the office.
Using the Modals Shall, Ought to and Should to Ask For Advice
You use the modals should and ought to express your opinion about what is right and what is wrong.
When you give advice, you are telling someone what you think is the right thing to do in a certain situation.
The most common modal for giving advice is should.

For example:
You really shouldn't be working so hard - you'll get sick!
You should get some rest over the weekend.

You can use ought to in the same sort of situations, but is sounds much more formal.

For example:

You ought to get some rest over the weekend.
You can use shall to ask for advice.

For example:
What shall I do?
Again, this sounds quite formal.

images.text:
Good lighting in workplaces is essential. Lighting should enable people to see clearly and perform their work safely. The key factors we ought to consider when determining the adequacy of lighting are:
the amount of light in an area;
the number, type and position of the light sources;
the tasks or activities performed.

In general, good lighting should enable employees to easily view their work and environment without the need to strain their eyes. However, different activities require different levels and qualities of light. The activity or task performed determines the lighting needs of an area. Activities, which do not require a high level of visual acuity shouldn't require levels or an optimum quality of light. On the other hand, tasks such as drawing or checking a document for errors involve fine and detailed work. These require a moderate to high level of work for your eyes, and so greater levels of light are required.

We are able to see quite well in a wide range of lighting levels due to the ability of the eye to adapt to different lighting conditions. For example, when you move from a bright room into a dark area, or vice versa, your eyes adapt and in a few seconds you are able to see more clearly. To reduce the demands on your eyes and the need to adapt when changing tasks or viewing fields, or when moving from one work area to another, specific levels of lighting for particular types of tasks are recommended.
